You can take a minute, and I will take off one, two.

Any more questions?
That is what I thought. Good evening.
That is my proposal for public safety.

meanings.note: Used both as a noun and as a formal vocative title in political debates.

examples.text: Eu passo a palavra ao candidato.
examples.trans: I give the floor to the candidate.

examples.text: Candidato, o senhor tem um minuto.

meanings.note: Marks the current moment resulting from an earlier action.

examples.trans: Now she is in a meeting.

examples.text: Agora tenho que resolver umas coisinhas.
examples.trans: Right now I have to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: Formed from real + -mente.

examples.text: Agora realmente o senhor passou dos limites.
examples.trans: Now you really crossed the line.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Polite title; saying sim, senhor to an equal coworker adds mock military obedience.

examples.trans: Are you going in now, sir?

meanings.note: Passar impune means to go unpunished; passar por means to undergo.

examples.text: Eles passam por muitos testes lá.
examples.trans: They go through many tests there.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: In um pouco (de), acts as a masculine quantifier noun meaning a little bit.

examples.text: O senhor passou um pouco dos limites.
examples.trans: You crossed the line a little.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
In passar dos limites, means to cross the line or go too far.
Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Literally 'obliged'; men say obrigado and women say obrigada.

examples.trans: Thank you very much, you hear?

meanings.note: Links verbs like faltar to an event or destination.
Everyday verb for removing or taking something out.

examples.trans: We took it out during surgery.

examples.text: Você tira o botão de baixo.
examples.trans: You take the button from the bottom.

meanings.note: Indefinite determiner or pronoun; plural alguns means some or a few.

examples.text: Alguns são bons, outros são ruins.
examples.trans: Some are good, others are bad.

meanings.note: A brief moment of time.
Possessive determiner agreeing with the possessed noun; in Brazil it most often means your (with você).

examples.text: É isso que você quer pra sua vida?
examples.trans: Is that what you want for your life?

meanings.note: Refers to someone's time or duration (esse tempo inteiro).

examples.text: Seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?
I stayed there that whole time.

poder.gloss: can; may; to be able to

meanings.en: can; may; to be able to
meanings.note: Core modal verb followed by an infinitive.

examples.text: O senhor pode ser meu fiador?
examples.trans: Can you be my guarantor, sir?

meanings.note: Unit of time; um minuto is standard debate timing.
All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Masculine cardinal numeral (feminine duas).

examples.trans: She is looking for two bedrooms.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.
Process of bargaining or negotiating terms.
Penalty imposed for breaking rules.
Marks comparisons (mais que), negated continuation (não ... mais, not anymore), and the farewell até mais.
In Portuguese, one 'makes' a question: fazer uma pergunta.

examples.text: O senhor pode fazer uma pergunta.

meanings.note: Regular -ar verb.
Everyday adjective in tá bom (okay), boa tarde (good afternoon), and Bom, pessoal (Well, folks).
Used in boa noite for both good evening on arrival and good night on departure.

examples.trans: A very good evening to everyone.

meanings.note: Demonstrative determiner; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese esse commonly covers both this near me and that just mentioned.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

examples.text: Vou ficar sentado esse tempo inteiro.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay seated that whole time.

meanings.note: First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?

meanings.note: A political proposal or business offer.
Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: In segurança pública, means public safety and policing.

examples.text: Essa é minha proposta pra segurança pública.
examples.trans: That is my proposal for public safety.

examples.text: A segurança do prédio é boa.

meanings.note: Modifies nouns like segurança pública (public safety).

examples.text: Essa é minha proposta pra segurança pública.
examples.trans: That is my proposal for public safety.

meanings.note: Everyday friendly farewell across Brazil, borrowed long ago from Italian ciao.
